key concepts of entity relationship
diagram, ERD, including the different

relationships between those entities,
cardinality, and crow's foot notation.
So, what exactly is an ERD? ERD stands
for entity relationship diagram. As the
name suggests, it represents the
entities involved in a business process
and the relationships between those
entities. Most of you already know that
the tables are referred to as entities
and the columns in those tables are
called attributes. That being said, the
real goal of data modeling is to
understand how different entities relate
to each other. For example, in a retail
hypermarket business, the main entities
could be customers, products, suppliers,
orders, and order items.
These entities interact with one or more
other entities based on the business
process flow. For instance, customers
place orders. Orders contain order line
items. Each order line item represents a
product. Products are supplied by
suppliers. And all these interactions
form what we call relationships. Now,
when we work on large real-world
projects, there are many stakeholders
involved. We have business users,
project managers, solution architects,
software engineers, testers, and many
others. We need a common way to
represent entities and relationships in
a simple, easy-to-understand graphical
form. Please take a look at the sample
data stored in these tables. Now, let me
ask you a simple question. Can you
clearly understand all the business
relationships just by looking at these?
You can probably identify the entities
involved, but you cannot confidently
tell how they are related to one
another. All right. Let's look at
something more technical. The create
table statements or DDLs used to define
these tables. Now, let me ask the same
question again. Can you clearly
understand all the business
relationships from this information? The
answer is still no. In fact, it becomes
even more difficult. The DDL contains a
lot of technical details that are
irrelevant to many stakeholders. This
clearly shows that we need a better and
more visual way to represent entities
and relationships. And that's exactly
where entity relationship diagrams come
into the picture. Take a look at this
ERD. Notice how clearly it shows the
entities involved and the relationships
between them. We'll discuss each of
these symbols and relationship notation
shortly. Even if you're not familiar
with all the symbols yet, you can still
start to understand how the entities are
linked together. But what is more
important is that ERDs provide a common
language that could be understood by all
project stakeholders, both technical and
non-technical. Designing and documenting
these diagrams in the early stages of a
project streamlines the process,
improves overall success, and reduces a
lot of rework later in the development
and testing phases. Now that we
understand why ERDs are important, let's
look at the different types of entities
and relationships along with the symbols
used to represent them. These symbols
are standard across the industry, and
having a clear understanding of them is
essential in any IT or data-driven
project. Now, when we talk about types
of entities in data modeling, they're
generally classified into three types.
The first type is a strong entity. A
strong entity is an entity that has its
own primary key and does not depend on
another entity for its identification.
For example, in our retail system,
customer, product, supplier, and order
are all strong entities because each of
them has its own primary key.
The second type is a weak entity. A weak
entity does not have its own primary
key. Instead, it relies entirely on a
parent entity for its identification.
For example, let's say we store a
customer's confidential information,
such as passport numbers, SSNs, and tax
IDs in a separate table called customer
sensitive info for security reasons.
This is a weak entity because if a
customer is removed from the system, the
corresponding customer sensitive info
record becomes completely invalid and
must be deleted. Similarly, a customer
address table is also a weak entity. We
generally split addresses into a
separate table because a single customer
might have multiple addresses, but those
addresses cannot exist in our system
without the customer.
The third type is an associative entity.
An associative entity is used to resolve
a many-to-many relationship between two
entities.
For example, in our retail system, a
product can be supplied by multiple
suppliers and a supplier can supply
multiple products.
This clearly forms a many-to-many
relationship, which creates design
problems if we do not introduce a link
table to break it. That link table is
what we call an associative entity.
Another good example is the order items
table. This is an associative entity
that breaks the many-to-many
relationship between orders and
products. If associative entity feels a
bit confusing, you can check out our
video on many-to-many relationships.
It's available in our data modeling
playlist linked in the description.
And these are the standard notations
used to represent each of these entity
types. A strong entity is represented
using a single rectangle. A weak entity
is represented using a double rectangle.
An associative entity is represented by
placing a diamond inside a rectangle.
Next, let's break down the different
types of relationships and their
corresponding notations in an ERD.
Before we look at the relationship
types, we should first understand what
cardinality means. Cardinality refers to
the number of rows in one entity that
can be associated with each row in
another entity. While this may feel a
bit confusing at first, the concept is
actually very simple. To understand
cardinality, we only need to remember
three possibilities: zero, one, and
many. These are represented using three
different symbols. A circle for zero, a
vertical line for one, and three
connected lines that resemble a crow's
foot for many. By combining these three
possibilities, we can represent all
relationship types in an ERD. Let's
start with a simple example between
customers and orders.
Whenever you look at a relationship,
focus on one side at a time and ask this
simple question. What is the minimum and
maximum number of records that could be
related to a single record on the other
side? Let's start from the customer
side. What is the minimum number of
customers a single order can be
associated with? The minimum is one.
Likewise, what is the maximum number of
customers a single order is associated
with? The maximum is also one. This
gives us a cardinality of one and only
one on the customer side. Now, let's
move to the order side. What is the
minimum number of orders a single
customer could have? Well, there could
be customers without any orders, so the
minimum is zero. What is the maximum
number of orders a single customer could
have? It can be as many as he or she
wishes. So, the maximum is many. This
gives us a cardinality of zero or many
on the order side. When we combine both
sides, we get a one and only one to zero
or many relationship between customers
and orders.
Let's take another example involving
orders and order items. Starting from
the order side, what is the minimum and
maximum number of orders a single order
item can be associated with? We all know
that an order item is tightly connected
to only one order. This gives us one and
only one on the order side. Now, let's
look at the order item side. What is the
minimum and maximum number of order
items a single order could have? Well,
each order should have a minimum of one
order item and a maximum of as many as
the customer needs. This gives us one or
many on the order item side. When we
combine both sides, we get a one and
only one to one or many relationship
between orders and order items.
Using the same approach, you can model
relationships between any number of
